title: Reading Codex 6 — Sessions Are Event Logs
description: Append-only JSON Lines, a scanner that reads backwards, and why resuming an agent is a reconstruction problem rather than a load.

lines.text: An agent session can run for hours. The process will die — crash, laptop lid, deliberate quit — and the question is what happens next. Whether you can pick the work back up is a persistence design decision, and it is one most homegrown agents get wrong by treating it as save the conversation to a file.
Codex has a whole crate for this, called rollout, plus a thread store on top of it.
The core format is append-only JSON Lines: one record per line, appended as things happen, never rewritten. A recorder writes items as the turn produces them.

Around that sits more machinery than you would expect. There is a session index and a reference index. There is compression, with an explicit step that materialises a compressed rollout back to plain lines before anything appends to it again. There is a SQLite state database alongside, used for metrics and search. There is maintenance, and a retention policy.
The detail I liked most is a module called the reverse JSON Lines scanner. It reads the file backwards. There is also a function to read just the head of a file for a summary.

And reconstruction is its own module in the session directory. It does not simply replay every record. It reasons about turn boundaries — deciding whether an item's turn identifier is compatible with the active turn, and finalising segments — and it rebuilds a context window from the recorded session state.

sections.title: Why it is built that way

lines.text: Take append-only first. The naive alternative is to hold conversation state in memory and write the whole thing out periodically. That loses everything since the last write when the process dies, and it has a much worse failure mode: a crash during the write leaves a truncated or corrupt file, so the crash that made you need the backup is the crash that destroys it. Appending complete lines means a crash costs you at most the line being written, and every earlier line is still valid.

Now the backwards scanner, because that is the one that shows real usage. What do you actually need from a session file most of the time? The most recent things. To list sessions you need each one's last activity and a summary. To resume you need the tail. Reading a multi-megabyte log forwards to get the last few records is wasteful, and it gets slower exactly as a session becomes more valuable. Reading backwards makes the common operation cost the same whether the session is ten minutes or ten hours old.
The head-read for summaries is the mirror image: the metadata you list sessions by is at the start, so read only that.

Then reconstruction. Here is why it is not a load. The log records what happened, including things you must not replay — a tool call that was cancelled, a turn that was interrupted mid-flight, output that was compacted away. Rebuilding the model's context is a different question from rebuilding the audit trail. The log is the truth of what occurred; the context window is a derived view, and deriving it means making decisions about partial turns.
That distinction — the log is history, the context is a projection of it — is the whole idea, and it is what event sourcing means in practice.

One more consequence worth drawing out, because it is the reason to care beyond crash recovery. Once the log is the truth, you can build things that were previously impossible: search across every session you have ever run, replay a session to debug why the agent did something last Tuesday, fork a session at a point and try a different path, and compute honest metrics about how often a tool fails.

None of that is available if state lives in memory and the file is a convenience. That is why the crate has a search module and a metrics database — those are not extras bolted on, they are what an event log makes cheap.
The minimum viable version is genuinely small and you should build it on day one, because retrofitting persistence into an agent that keeps state in variables is miserable.

Append one JSON object per line, per event, as it happens. Flush. Do not buffer to look clever. Include a turn identifier and a timestamp on every record — you cannot reconstruct turn boundaries later if you did not record them.

Keep the reconstruction function separate from the recording function, and make it explicit that it is building a projection. Even if version one just replays everything, having the seam there means handling interrupted turns is a change in one place.
Add the backwards read when listing sessions gets slow, not before. It is thirty lines and it is easy to add later; it is only worth doing once you have long sessions.
Skip compression, the SQLite index and retention policy until you have enough sessions that finding one is a problem. Those are answers to having thousands of them.

One trap to avoid, since it is easy to walk into. Do not write the model's context window to disk as your log. It is tempting, because it is right there and it is already the shape you need on resume. But the context is lossy by design — compaction has already thrown things away — so you would be persisting the projection and discarding the history. Log the events; derive the context.

The one idea: your session log is an append-only record of what happened, and the model's context is a projection derived from it. Conflate the two and resume will quietly replay things that should never happen twice.
